Practicing this dharma proceeds from twenty-two categories down to four, three, two, and one, totaling eighty-one categories; from this dharma emerge the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the meditative absorption of cessation, totaling ninety receptivities (kṣānti).
"Below all merits" is the fourth section, which serves as a summary.

Furthermore, there are ten million billion *brahmās* of the nine Brahma realms, the three Pure Abodes, the three Radiant Heavens, and the five Heavens of Joy; they possess the constant bliss of celestial concentration, the flavor of meditative merit, and supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), having fully accomplished the merits of the eighteen places of rebirth.
The seventh column is the Brahmakāyika devas, which has four parts:
first, a general indication of the number; second, a specific enumeration of their names and numbers; third, a praise of their virtues; and fourth, a concluding summary.
Regarding the first, because the number is ten thousand times ten thousand, it is said to be "ten trillion" (wan-wan-yi).
Below "three pure" (*śubha*), the second section lists the specific numbers.
The "three pure" refers to the three heavens of the third dhyāna, namely: Limited Purity (*parītta-śubha*), Immeasurable Purity (*apramāṇa-śubha*), and Universal Purity (*śubha-kṛtsna*).
The "three lights" refers to the three heavens of the second dhyāna, namely: Limited Light (*parītta-ābhā*), Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇa-ābhā*), and Light-Sound (*ābhāsvara*).
The "three Brahmā realms" refer to the three heavens of the first dhyāna: first, the Brahmakāyika; second, the Brahmapurohita; and third, the Mahābrahmā.

Regarding the "five heavens of joy and bliss," there are nine heavens in the fourth dhyāna: first, the Parīttaśubha; second, the Apramāṇaśubha; third, the Śubhakṛtsna; and fourth, the Anabhraka. These four heavens are not discussed here; only the latter five are listed.

The five "Joyful Abodes" (Sukhāvatī) refer to the five Pure Abode Heavens (*śuddhāvāsakāyika*). Because the inhabitants of these realms delight in discussing the meaning of the Dharma, they are called "Joyful. They are: first, Avṛha; second, Atapa; third, Sudarśana; fourth, Sudṛśa; and fifth, Akaniṣṭha.
Below "Heavenly Determined Merit" (*deva-niyata-guṇa*) is the third section, the Praise of Merit.
"Heavenly determined" refers to fixed retribution; that is, the dhyāna of retribution and the five aggregates of retribution.
"Merit determined" refers to pure concentration; that is, the pure dhyāna and the wholesome, out-flowing five aggregates.
"Relishing flavors" refers to the concentration of relishing flavors, which is attachment to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
"Constantly delighting in supernormal powers" refers to the two types of supernormal powers: those acquired through cultivation and those obtained as a karmic retribution.
The merits of all eighteen places of birth are fully accomplished; this summarizes the eighteen heavens of the aforementioned four dhyānas.

Furthermore, there are billions upon billions of sons of the gods in the six desire realms, who have fully accomplished the supernatural powers and merits that are the retributions for the ten wholesome actions.
The eighth row consists of the six classes of devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which has four parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; third, the praise of their virtues; and fourth, the summary conclusion.
Regarding the initial phrase "billions upon billions," this refers to a cumulative count of billions.
Among the six heavens of the desire realm, this is the second list of names.
The Four Heavenly Kings are: in the east, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which means "Lord Who Sustains the Nation";
in the south, Virūḍhaka, which means "Lord of Increase."
In the west is Virūpākṣa, which is translated here as "Lord of Varied Speech";
in the north is Vaiśravaṇa, which is translated here as "Lord of Much Hearing.
These two [preside over] the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is translated here as "Heaven of Playful Joy," and is also called the "Thirty-three Heavens."
Third is the Yāma Heaven; this is translated as "Good Portion" (Śubhakṛtsna) and is also called "Good Time.
Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven; this is translated as "Contentment.
Fifth is the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, where one enjoys oneself with pleasure-objects created by oneself.

The sixth is the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*); because they freely enjoy the five objects of desire and the implements of pleasure emanated by others, it is named "Making Use of Others' Emanations.
Below the ten wholesome deeds is the third section, which praises their virtues.
Not giving rise to the ten evils constitutes the ten virtues; because one obtains the retribution of the six heavens, it is called the "retribution of the ten virtues.
The phrase "all merits are accomplished" below marks the fourth section, which is the general conclusion.

Furthermore, there were sixteen great kings, each with a retinue of ten thousand, twenty thousand, or even up to one hundred thousand followers; through the merit of the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the three refuges, they were fully endowed with pure faith and conduct.
The ninth assembly, the multitude of kings, also has four parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the clarification of their retinues; third, the praise of their virtues; and fourth, the summary conclusion.
Regarding the first part, the mention of "sixteen kingdoms" constitutes the enumeration.
"Each and every one below" clarifies the retinue.
"The five precepts and ten wholesome actions below" is a threefold praise of virtue.

Regarding the merit of the Three Refuges: before the Buddha appeared in the world, people took refuge in and paid homage to the heterodox Three Jewels—the various heavens and heterodox teachers as the Buddha Jewel, the four Vedas and so forth as the Dharma Jewel, and the various non-Buddhist practitioners as the Sangha Jewel.
Only when the Tathāgata appears in the world do people turn to and revere the Threefold True Jewel.
A practitioner of pure faith is so called because they have accomplished the four kinds of faith;
furthermore, they are named "pure faith" because they universally attain the correct faith of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding "endowment," it refers to being endowed with the fourfold faith in the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings of the five destinies;
the tenth [section] lists the multitudes of these five destinies.
Or, those who have been able to come to this Dharma assembly through the power of the Sage’s compassion should be categorized among the six paths;
asuras are included within the path of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable multitudes from other directions.
The eleventh row consists of the holy assemblies from other directions;
the textual description is clear.

Furthermore, there are transformed pure lands of the ten directions appearing with ten billion high seats, and ten billion precious *sumeru*-like lotus flowers are manifested. Before each seat, upon the flowers, are immeasurable transformation Buddhas, along with immeasurable bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and the great assembly of the eight classes of beings, each sitting upon a precious lotus flower. Above each flower, there are immeasurable lands.
The twelfth row consists of the assembly of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
These are inconceivable bodhisattvas; therefore, they are able to transform the pure lands and the assemblies of Buddhas of the ten directions, bringing them to this land.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, it explains how the inconceivable power can transform the land;
second, from "There are immeasurable... onwards, it explains how the inconceivable power can manifest Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Each of the three hundred and ten Buddhas descends individually to manifest their inconceivable power capable of preaching the Prajñāpāramitā.
First, regarding the manifestation of the transformation of the lands, the text says "the ten directions," which refers to the six cardinal directions along with the four intermediate points.
“Pure Land” refers, for example, to the Western Pure Land.
“Ten billion” refers to ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion Mount Sumerus.
From the passage “There are immeasurable transformation Buddhas” downward, the second section clarifies how the inconceivable power can manifest Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The subsequent explanation of the eight assemblies is as follows: first, the assembly of kṣatriyas; second, the assembly of śramaṇas; third, the assembly of brahmins; fourth, the assembly of the Four Great Kings; fifth, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; sixth, the assembly of the gods of the six heavens of desire; seventh, the assembly of Māra; and eighth, the assembly of Brahmā.
Furthermore, regarding the eight classes of beings, including the nāgas and ghosts: first, the gandharvas; second, the piśācas—these two belong to the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
third, the kumbhāṇḍas; fourth, the pretas—these two belong to the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka; fifth, the nāgas;
sixth, the pūtanas—these two belong to the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa.
The seventh are named yakṣas and the eighth are named rākṣasas; these two belong to the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
In each and every land, the Buddha and his great assembly were no different from those present here today.

Within each and every land, each Buddha and their respective great assemblies each preached the Prajñāpāramitā. The great assemblies from other directions, the manifested assemblies, and the assemblies within these three realms—the twelve great assemblies—all came together in conclave. They sat upon lotus thrones that endure for nine kalpas; the assembly was square and vast, measuring nine hundred and fifty li, and the great multitude sat there in solemn unison.

As for each Buddha and their respective great assemblies each preaching the Prajñāpāramitā, this refers to the power of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*) and the inconceivable power (*acintyabala*) to expound the Dharma.
The preceding section has concluded the separate enumeration of the twelve assemblies.
Below the phrase "the great assembly from other directions," there is a separate enumeration of the second summary regarding the number of members within the twelve assemblies.
The term "the great assembly from other directions" summarizes the second assembly mentioned previously, that of those from other directions.
The phrase "as for those who transform the assembly" concludes the third section concerning the transformed assembly.
The phrase "within these three realms" concludes the first section concerning the twelve assemblies of this world.
The mention of the "twelve assemblies" summarizes the three preceding assemblies.
The "nine-layered lotus throne" refers to a nine-tiered flower seat.
Regarding the measurement of nine hundred and fifty *li*, it is like the assembly at the Twin Trees, where twelve *yojanas* could accommodate a vast multitude.
The present assembly is likewise; though it is limited in scope, it accommodates a great many people.
As for the fact that the great multitude all sit together, they are all seated to listen to the Dharma.
Question:
Why is it that among the various devas there are those who do not hear the Dharma, yet they come from the three miserable realms to receive the Way?
Answer:
Master Zhizhe of Tiantai said:

Regarding this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, laxity in regard to the precepts is not what is called "laxity"; rather, laxity in regard to the Vehicle is what is called "laxity. Concerning this, one may establish a fourfold classification:

there are those who are urgent regarding the Vehicle but lax regarding the precepts; those who are urgent regarding the precepts but lax regarding the Vehicle; those who are urgent in both; and those who are lax in both.

They were born in the heavens because they observed the precepts and cultivated meditative concentration in the past; yet they could not hear the sutras because they did not cultivate wisdom in the past.

As for those who come from the three miserable realms to receive the Way, they fell into the three realms because they violated the precepts, but they are summoned by the sound and light because they cultivated wisdom in past lives.
Both the simultaneous urgency and the simultaneous relaxation can be known.

At that time, the Buddha Śākyamuni—endowed with the ten titles, the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*), and the great extinction-truth (*mahā-nirodha-satya*)—on the eighth day of the first month, sat upon the tenth stage and entered the samādhi of the Great Chamber of Quiescence.
Regarding the "Ten Epithets" at that time, the following section explains the temporal setting of the sutra.
This consists of seven parts: first, the section clarifying the Tathāgata’s entry into *samādhi*;

second, the emission of light; third, the manifestation of flowers; fourth, the shaking of the earth; fifth, the posing of questions; sixth, the performance of music, the praise of the Buddha, and the summoning of the assemblies from the ten directions to gather; and seventh, the emergence from *samādhi*.
The first entry into meditative concentration occurs within the stage of *samādhi*.
"At that time" refers to that very moment.
The ten titles manifest his virtues, causing sentient beings to take refuge.
The "Threefold Knowledge" (trividyā) signifies the perfect discernment of the three periods of time and the precise understanding of the capacities of sentient beings.
"Great Extinction" (mahānirvāṇa) praises the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment; it signifies that he is himself unbound and is able to liberate others.
"Vajra" praises the Buddha's wisdom and virtue.
Furthermore, "at that time" refers to the moment when he was about to preach the Dharma.
The "Ten Epithets" signify that his name and virtues were renowned far and wide, inspiring the faith and devotion of all beings.
The three insights (*trividyā*) manifest the discernment of the faculties and natures of sentient beings.
Great extinction (*mahānirvāṇa*) is precisely *nirvāṇa*.
The vajra is not the vajra within the causal stage; it is the vajra-path wisdom of the seed-nature (*vajramārgabījajñāna*) at the ultimate stage of fruition.
Śākyamuni means "The Able Benevolent One" (Nengren).
Each Buddha manifests his name through a specific virtue; for example, Maitreya is named the "Kindly One" (Cishi). Since which Buddha lacks kindness?
This one is thus named after kindness, and is called Maitreya.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata was also like this.
Regarding the "eighth day of the first month," this clarifies the specific time and season:

he preached this sutra on the eighth day of the first month in the thirty-sixth year after his enlightenment; it was only seven years after his enlightenment that he preached the other Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.

According to various textual records, from the twenty-ninth year until the present time, it should have been thirty-six years since his attainment of enlightenment; thus, he preached this sūtra at the age of sixty-six, having attained enlightenment at sixty.

Regarding the statement "only now sitting on the tenth stage," it means that because his causal practices were perfected, he has realized the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, he is said to be "now sitting on the tenth stage.
This refers back to his former causes and does not mean that he is only beginning to sit [on the stages] now.

It is further stated: "These are the ten stages of the Buddha: first, the Stage of Profound Depth, Difficult to Know, and Vast Wisdom-Virtue; second, the Stage of the Inconceivable Pure Body; third, the Ocean-Treasury Stage; fourth, the Stage of Supernatural Powers and Wisdom-Virtue; fifth, the Stage of Radiant Virtue; sixth, the Stage of the Manifestation of the Stainless Flame-Light; seventh, the Stage of the Vast and Supreme Dharma-Dhātu-Treasury and Radiant Realm; eighth, the Stage of Unobstructed Wisdom; ninth, the Stage of Boundless Hundred-Million Adornments, Dedication, and Illumination; tenth, the Stage of the Vairocana-Wisdom-Treasury. This is from the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (or *Dharmatā-viśeṣa-sūtra*).

Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata must first enter meditative concentration before preaching the Dharma" when entering the chamber of great stillness: he enters concentration in order to observe the capacities of beings and examine the underlying principles.

Since one wishes to clarify that the Tathāgata is eternally quiescent while constantly active, and eternally active while constantly quiescent, how could there be any distinction between entering and emerging from concentration?
From the eighth stage upward, there is no entering or arising from meditative absorption; how could the Tathāgata have such entering and arising?

This is shown to provide a model for the world: if even the Tathāgata enters meditative absorption to contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā, how much more so should other people not speak without reflection?

As he contemplates this object, he emits great rays of light that illuminate the three realms; furthermore, from the crown of his head, a thousand precious lotuses emerge, their blossoms reaching as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, and the light likewise extends even to the Buddha-lands of other directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The text states that "contemplation is the condition" (*cintā-pratyaya*). This means that the greatest teaching arises from the condition of great wisdom’s clear discernment; therefore, it is called "contemplation as the condition.
Furthermore, another interpretation of "contemplation as the condition" is that when one wishes to expound the *prajñā*, one contemplates the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*).
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the passage "emitting great radiance," this is the second section within the description of the timing of the preaching of the sutra, clarifying the emission of light.

This "great radiance" manifests rare and marvelous events, causing those who have not yet developed faith to do so, and enabling those who already possess faith to attain further increase. It is also intended to cause sentient beings to shatter the darkness of ignorance and attain the illumination of wisdom.
There are two kinds of light:
first, the light of supernormal powers (ṛddhi); second, the light of wisdom (prajñā).
For what reason does he emit the light of supernormal powers?

However, my children who possess the necessary conditions are scattered throughout the ten directions; if I do not emit light to summon them, they will not know the causes and conditions for preaching the Prajñāpāramitā. This is why I emit this light.
He emits the light of wisdom because he discerns the characteristics of phenomena in accordance with the faculties and capacities of sentient beings.
"Illuminating that which is within the three realms" refers to the extent reached by this light.
Furthermore, "the lotus flower atop his head" refers to the third supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
Some perceive light and thereby trigger their spiritual potential, while others see flowers and thereby attain benefit; for this reason, he manifests flowers.
"Reaching upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception" refers to the extent to which the flowers reach.
This sutra clarifies that there is form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"The light is likewise" means it is identical to the flower.
"Even unto other directions" means that it not only illuminates this direction, but also pervades the ten directions.
"Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" signifies that the paths of transformation and teaching are mutually interconnected.

At that time, from the Formless Realm, immeasurable transformations of great fragrant flowers rained down; the fragrance was like chariot wheels and the flowers were like Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, descending like clouds.
Regarding those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) at that time, some interpret this by saying:
"Although there is no coarse form in the formless realm, there exists subtle form.
This interpretation is not correct.
Because form and formlessness are characterized by neither form nor non-form, it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
When the gods of the Form and Desire Realms heard the Prajñāpāramitā, they rejoiced and rained down flowers as an offering.
Within this, there are three parts: first, the devas of the formless realm rain flowers; second, the devas of the form realm rain flowers; third, the six heavens of the desire realm rain flowers.

Regarding the rain of flowers from the formless realm, there are three subordinate phrases: first, they rain immeasurable great fragrant flowers; second, the fragrance is like that of a chariot wheel; third, the flowers are like Mount Sumeru, descending like clouds.
The eighteen Brahma kings rained down flowers of a hundred extraordinary colors, while the devas of the six heavens of desire rained down flowers of immeasurable colors.
Before the Buddha’s seat, nine hundred trillion kalpa-flowers spontaneously arose, reaching upward as far as the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
Eighteenth: Below, in the second [section], the devas of the Form Realm rain flowers of a hundred transformed colors;

in the third, regarding the rain of flowers from the devas of the Desire Realm, it first clarifies the immeasurable flowers, next clarifies the flowers produced throughout nine hundred trillion kalpas, and finally clarifies the extent to which these flowers reach.

First, he emitted light, desiring to cause sentient beings to shatter darkness and attain illumination; next, he manifested flowers, desiring to cause sentient beings to cultivate the causes and attain the fruits.
At that time, the earth of this world shook in six ways.
Regarding the statement that at this time the earth of the world shook in six ways: this is the fourth supernatural power, the shaking of the earth.
For what reason is the earth shaken?
It is because one wishes to shake the minds of sentient beings who cling to the notion of "attainment," so as to cause them to awaken to the *prajñā* of non-attainment.

The six kinds of shaking are: the east surges while the west subsides; the west surges while the east subsides; the south surges while the north subsides; the north surges while the south subsides; the periphery surges while the center subsides; and the center surges while the periphery subsides.

Another interpretation is that, as stated in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*, there are six [types of movement]: shaking (*calana*), surging (*prācalana*), trembling (*sampracalana*), rising (*udvega*), crashing (*kṣubdhana*), and roaring (*raṇa*).
This concludes the first fascicle of the *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
